topic: McGurk & MacDonald (1976): Hearing Voices Your Ears Never Received — How Vision Rewrites Speech ('BA' + 'GA' = 'DA')
visual_mode_reason: Harry McGurk and John MacDonald's accidental 1976 dubbing discovery ('ba-ba' audio + 'ga-ga' lips = unmistakable 'da-da' heard by 98% of adults!) is a foundational multisensory brain fusion phenomenon driven by superior temporal sulcus / auditory-visual integration.

primary_case.title: Harry McGurk & John MacDonald's 1976 Nature 'Hearing Lips and Seeing Voices' dubbing experiment
primary_case.place: Department of Psychology, University of Surrey, Guildford, UK

people.name: Harry McGurk & John MacDonald
people.role: Developmental psychologists studying infant perception at Surrey who asked a technician to dub mismatched syllables onto video — and couldn't believe their own ears.

people.name: Technician in the Surrey AV suite
people.role: Created the split audio-video dub ('ba-ba' sound onto 'ga-ga' lip movements) that fooled both researchers into thinking the audio track had been recorded wrong

people.name: Michael S. Beauchamp & Nath
people.role: Neuroscientists who localized human McGurk audiovisual fusion to the posterior Superior Temporal Sulcus (pSTS) and proved TMS disruption of pSTS turns 'da' right back into 'ba'.

core_facts.fact: In 1976 at the University of Surrey, Harry McGurk and John MacDonald were testing how infants respond when a mother's voice comes from a different spot than her face, and asked a video technician to dub the sound **'ba-ba'** onto a close-up film of a woman's lips pronouncing **'ga-ga'**.

When McGurk and MacDonald played the dubbed video back, neither heard 'ba' OR 'ga' — both swore the loudspeaker was clearly saying **'DA-DA'**. They scolded the technician for mixing up the audio until they closed their eyes — and the exact same speaker instantly said **'BA-BA'**.

Testing 103 participants across three age brackets (3-to-4-year-olds, 7-to-8-year-olds, and 18-to-40-year-old adults, Nature 1976), **98% of adults** (and 59-81% of young children) reported hearing the fused phantom third syllable **'da'** when watching 'ga' lips over 'ba' sound.

Even more bizarre was the reverse pairing: dubbing **'ga-ga' audio** onto **'ba-ba' lip closure** didn't fuse into a middle consonant — majorities heard the double-consonant combination **'bagba'** or **'gaba'** because visibly sealed lips ('b') cannot logically produce a back-throat 'g' alone.

Knowing the trick gives ZERO immunity: Harry McGurk himself knew every frame of the dub, yet opening his eyes flipped his conscious hearing from 'ba' to 'da' every single time for the rest of his life.

Remarkably, visual speech starts entering the brain ~100-150 milliseconds BEFORE sound hits the cochlea (because lip shaping precedes vocal-cord vibration), letting visual cortex prime auditory cortex and posterior temporal lobe in advance.

In 2010, Michael Beauchamp, Audrey Nath, and colleagues delivered single-pulse Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (TMS) strictly over left posterior Superior Temporal Sulcus (pSTS) right during the syllable: temporarily silencing pSTS abolished the McGurk illusion so subjects heard the true acoustic 'ba' again — without hurting normal single-sense hearing or vision.

Modern replications (Tiippana, Alsius, Van Engen, SRC3) revealed fascinating individual differences: some healthy adults fuse 95% of trials while others fuse <20% depending on pSTS connectivity, native language phonology (e.g., quieter face-gaze cultures like Japanese show weaker baseline McGurk unless background noise rises), and noisy-room reliance.

wow_facts.fact: Close your eyes and the loudspeaker says **'BA — BA — BA'** with 100% clarity; open your eyes to watch lips mouthing **'GA — GA — GA'**, and your own ears swear the speaker switched to **'DA — DA — DA'** — 98% of adults in McGurk's 1976 paper got fooled.
wow_facts.why_surprising: You don't hear with your ears alone; you hear with your eyes.

wow_facts.fact: Even the two scientists who DISCOVERED the illusion thought their studio technician had botched the audio dub until they covered the TV screen with their hands.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Conscious knowledge cannot override automatic pSTS sensory fusion.

wow_facts.fact: Pause the posterior Superior Temporal Sulcus for 100 milliseconds with harmless magnetic stimulation (Beauchamp 2010), and the phantom 'DA' vanishes instantly — restoring raw 'BA' while leaving eyesight and hearing 100% sharp.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Causal proof of the exact cortical weld point between sight and sound.

wow_facts.fact: Because lips visibly move ~120 milliseconds BEFORE vocal cords buzz, watching a speaker's face in a noisy restaurant acts like a free 15-decibel hearing-aid boost.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Everyday speech comprehension is secretly audiovisual.

misconceptions.myth: Hearing happens strictly along a sealed pipe from ear cochlea to auditory cortex.
misconceptions.truth: Visual lip geometry reaches posterior temporal and even early auditory cortex milliseconds before sound finishes arriving, co-authoring what you consciously 'hear'.

misconceptions.myth: Once someone explains an illusion, your brain stops falling for it.
misconceptions.truth: Just like Muller-Lyer lines in vision, McGurk fusion runs below conscious belief — open your eyes, 'da'; close your eyes, 'ba'.

misconceptions.myth: Every human being experiences 100% McGurk fusion on every clip regardless of speaker or culture.
misconceptions.truth: Modern massive replications show wide healthy person-to-person variation in pSTS audiovisual weighting and stronger visual pull whenever acoustic noise rises.

everyday_hooks: Turning on subtitles or putting on your glasses at a loud party and swearing 'Wait — suddenly I can HEAR people better!'
Feeling strangely exhausted trying to catch words on an audio-only conference call with choppy microphones vs clear video.
Opening and closing your eyes during a 5-second 'BA/GA — DA' clip and gasping as the consonant flips mid-sentence.
